item.title: A problem with alot of scp articles.: Re: A problem with alot of scp articles.
item.content:encoded:
SCP-914 is an older writing (from series 1), and primarily since a lot of nostalgia surrounds it, it's less likely to be edited.
To explain why some information is censored (or "redacted" as many it's often called), that's actually to serve as a narrative ( someone off-site mentioned that the lore is supposed to mean that the reader is supossedly accessing confidential information, and thus is their own character).
Try to read some newer SCP's and see if there's any difference, as newer entries tend to have a different feel to them. They may be written with less common language.

item.title: Architecture of sites and areas: Re: Architecture of sites and areas
item.content:encoded:
My headcanon is that you might have a lobby where the place looks a little better or a major campus-type site might have a fancy front office building for impressing politicians or representatives, but outside that sites are designed by engineers, not architects.

That is, the office and light lab areas have that look where you can swap hallways between any generic office, academic campus, research facility, government building or hospital by changing the colors of the walls and tile. You can furnish your office, cubicle, and/or quarters as you like (within reason), and there's obviously going to be human touches like plants in empty corners and parrot streamers left up in the lounge from last year's luau-themed staff cookout, but for the structure itself, the key word is "pragmatic". Cubicle farms and copy-paste design are the rule, and you wouldn't see much difference between low-security humanoid containment cells and quarters for resident staff.

Hardened lab and high security areas drop even that much accommodation to comfort-
+ and are where the concept-development side of my brain really kicks in.
- Cue Danny Elfman Music:

The standard architecture for a mass storage site is a three dimensional grid of reinforced columns, bulkheads, and crossmembers, spaced with redundant support capacity in expectation that sooner or later something is going breach and take a bunch of them with it. Concrete, refractory brick, and powder-painted steel are the materials of choice; convoluted networks of pipes and cables line the walls and ceilings. These areas tend to be underground with floorspace most relatably measured in city blocks.

Need a few humanoid containment chambers? Fill in a cube of support columns, add subdivisions, doors and catwalks as needed. Need a bigger room? Tear down a wall or two, annex a section of hallway.

Sites of this sort almost inevitably become winding mazes of hallways threaded between chambers, with near constant construction and reconstruction going on as new anomalies are contained and the needs of existing ones shift. Following pipes marked with yellow triangles or green "5"s is often the most reliable means of navigation, and periodic reviews are done to separate genuine reports of structural anomalies from hallways that disappeared due to renovation.

item.title: A problem with alot of scp articles.: Re: A problem with alot of scp articles.
item.content:encoded:
They aren't actual scientific reports, they're short stories. We're a creative writing website. People will overlook some inaccuracies or a bit of casual language if the story is good enough, especially given that relatively few of the people on the site are actual scientists.

(Also, censorship makes sense of a clandestine organisation, but more importantly when done well it can serve a narrative purpose.)

Edit: Also, draft reviewers? 1) Generally very well versed in clinical tone despite most being non-scientists, 2) are doing difficult time-consuming work for free, 3) are often addressing much larger writing problems, and 4) have no control over what authors actually post.

item.title: How do Type Greens come to be?: Re: How do Type Greens come to be?
item.content:encoded:
There's a bit of info about their skill progression here, from a GOC perspective.

The Hume FAQ might also interest you. It also has a lot of links to reality-bender SCPs.

Personally I think for your "standard" type greens, it's mostly genetic, and their powers develop as they age.

Alternate idea, in abnormal psychology we have a thing we call the diathesis-stress model, where someone might have a "risk factor" like certain genes, but this is only "activated" by a major stressor/situation.

However, IMO there are infinite possible sources for anomalies, so you might very well see someone else with nearly-identical powers that were given to them by a God, a deal with the devil, or radiation, or magic or whatever. It's kinda up to you.

Edit: You can also use Tag Search in the bar on the left and search for ontokinetic and humanoid to find relevant SCPs.

item.title: What award would somebody get for neutralizing a keter?: Re: What award would somebody get for neutralizing a keter?
item.content:encoded:
Well, there's the Foundation Star, as shown here: SCP-1983. However, they were only rewarded for the neutralization given that this was an incredibly dangerous anomaly that was quite possibly impossible to contain and chewing up agents.

You could also say that readers didn't mind them breaking that "rule" because it was a good story.

IMO, if your story is about a reality bender being awarded for accidentally neutralizing a anomaly (which most readers don't think would be rewarded), and you're just picking between the most well-known Keters on the site, maybe read more of the wiki? That might be a hard story to pull off unless you have more lore to build from and know what current readers enjoy.

Does this count as necroposting?

Technically yes, but it's only a problem if the conversation is long past over and/or the new reply is relatively contentless.

In this case, the thread is still active and questions are still being actively answered, plus your response presents new information to the conversation, so you're fine here.
